newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt steps in to give Mideast peace talks a push.
newsitem.headline: Egypt steps in to give Mideast peace talks a push.

text.p: Egypt has stepped up diplomatic activity to try to advance the stalled Middle East peace talks because no one else was doing the pushing, analysts and diplomats said on Wednesday.

Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak's senior political adviser Osama al-Baz is due to leave for Israel and the Palestinian self-rule areas on Thursday for another round of shuttle diplomacy with the leadership of the two sides.

Baz has had separate meetings with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Palestinian President Yasser Arafat several times recently and hosted talks between negotiators from both sides in Cairo on Sunday to try to do what U.S. and European Union (EU) envoys could not -- get the peace process back on track.

"Egypt is playing a greater role now because of the self-marginalisation of the much-needed American role. The American definition of that role is totally out of line with that of a co-sponsor of peace. America is reacting to events and that is not enough," an Arab analyst in Cairo told Reuters.

Arabs have decried what they see as a greatly reduced U.S. effort to jump-start negotiations through the efforts of envoys and are dismayed by U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright's perceived reluctance to visit the region.

The EU decision to contribute its own envoy to peace efforts was at first welcomed by Arabs, who see the EU as siding with the Palestinians against the United States' pro-Israeli line, but it became clear it could not match Washington's clout.

"The Europeans talk about a role but they're unable to define that role in a practical manner that is operational," said Ibrahim Karawan, head of the Middle East programme at the International Institute for Strategic Studies in London.

"There is a growing awareness of the dangers of leaving the situation as it has been developing. It is in that setting that Egypt appeared to be the most likely candidate to provide a setting for the resumption of the effort, at least to renew the peace talks," he told Reuters.
Talks between Palestinians and Israel broke down in March after the Jewish state started to build a Jewish settlement in Arab East Jerusalem.

Arafat demands an end to the settlement building, Netanyahu has vowed to continue and both sides refuse to budge. Enter Cairo to give them a nudge by setting up the first formal talks between the two sides in two months in Cairo on Sunday.

"Egypt was concerned that things were not moving and that something had to be done. There was complete deadlock," said a Western diplomat in Cairo. "There's quite a gap to bridge but simply the fact that we have the two sides starting talks is more positive than what was happening before."
Egypt in 1979 became the first Arab state to sign a peace treaty with Israel and has since mediated unofficially between Palestinians and Israelis.

Arab countries boycotted Egypt for almost a decade for that peace deal but the Cairo government has since become one of the greatest champions of the Palestinians in their often arduous talks with Israel.

Egypt became especially outspoken in its criticism of the Jewish state after Netanyahu came to power last June, strongly criticising his right-wing views, particularly on continuing to build Jewish settlements on occupied or disputed land.
But analysts and diplomats said they did not think Egypt's pro-Palestinian line would hinder its role as honest broker in the attempt to relaunch peace talks.

"Egypt's bias is there in the Israeli perception but it is something useful because Egypt can exert more useful pressure on the Palestinians than the U.S. could," another Western diplomat in Cairo told Reuters.
"This is a reason to value Egypt's role rather than criticise it. I think Israeli is happy with the change, with Egypt moving away from isolating Israel into a mediating role," the diplomat said.
An Arab analyst said: "Because of its traditional, cultural and historical background, Egypt can't be equidistant but it doesn't have to be in order to play the role of honest broker."
But analysts say Egypt's efforts must end in more than a face-saving formula to rescue the two sides from their entrenched positions.

"It's important not to rely too much on what (former U.S. Secretary of State Henry) Kissinger used to call constructive ambiguity or a deal that allows you to say that you won and allows your main rivals to claim they won too," said Karawan.

"It is important to know where we are heading instead of saying that as long as the train seems to be moving then we are better off. The question is -- in which direction is the train moving?" he added.
